narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your class ranking at the end of your third year. Placing in the second decile is substantially lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. This single factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 34 was the second most important feature. While this score is only a few points below the 37.2 average of accepted students, the model still interpreted it as a moderate push toward passing rather than failing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.6 had a similar but smaller positive effect; it nudged the prediction slightly toward success, yet it was not enough to overcome the earlier academic ranking.

In short, the model concluded that your relatively low year-three class standing outweighed the modest positive signals from your test score and college grades.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen your academic record where it matters most. Retake challenging courses, aim for top-decile performance in future semesters, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise your score meaningfully. These targeted improvements will directly address the factors that led to your current rejection.
